lesson.title: Quality Factor: Grading How Sharply a Circuit Resonates
lesson.summary: Quality factor Q compares a resonant circuit's stored energy to its dissipated energy, and equivalently equals resonant frequency divided by bandwidth.
lesson.body:
Quality factor, written Q, is a single dimensionless number that grades how sharply a resonant circuit responds around its resonant frequency, and it is built directly from two quantities covered earlier in this unit: bandwidth and resonant frequency. The definition is Q equals omega_0 divided by the bandwidth, where omega_0 is the resonant angular frequency. A large Q means a narrow bandwidth relative to the resonant frequency, a sharp, tall response; a small Q means a wide bandwidth relative to resonant frequency, a broad, shallow response.

For a series RLC circuit there are several equivalent formulas for Q, and it is worth checking that they all agree, because that agreement is itself the proof that the definitions are consistent. Using the same circuit from the bandwidth chapter, R equals 100 ohms, L equals 1 H, C equals 1 microfarad, with omega_0 equals 1000 rad/s and bandwidth equals 100 rad/s: directly from the definition, Q equals omega_0 over BW equals 1000 over 100, which is 10. From the formula Q equals omega_0 L over R, Q equals 1000 times 1, divided by 100, which is also 10. From the formula Q equals 1 over (omega_0 R C), Q equals 1 divided by (1000 times 100 times 0.000001), which is 1 divided by 0.1, again 10. And from Q equals (1 over R) times the square root of L over C, Q equals (1 over 100) times the square root of (1 divided by 0.000001), which is (1 over 100) times the square root of 1,000,000, or (1 over 100) times 1000, once more exactly 10. Four different formulas, one consistent answer.

Physically, Q compares energy stored to energy lost. At resonance, energy sloshes back and forth between the inductor's magnetic field and the capacitor's electric field, while the resistor steadily drains a little of that energy away as heat on every cycle. Formally, Q equals 2 pi times the maximum energy stored, divided by the energy dissipated in one full cycle. A high Q circuit, like an LC tank built with very low resistance, loses very little energy per cycle relative to what it holds, so it keeps ringing for a long time and its resonance peak is narrow and tall. A low Q circuit dissipates a large fraction of its stored energy every cycle, so the oscillation dies out quickly and its resonance peak is wide and shallow. The Q of 10 found here is a moderate value, typical of many practical filters, neither razor sharp nor barely resonant, and it is exactly the number the next two chapters use to describe what actually happens at and around resonance.
